title: Predict
question: What is a language model trying to do?
what: A language model assigns probabilities to possible next tokens, given the text so far. A token is a piece of text: we will start with individual characters.
why: One small, repeated task gives us a way to learn from ordinary text. The next character in the training text supplies the answer; we do not need to label every example by hand.
exampleTitle: A prediction is a set of possibilities
example: Possible next characters: t, r, n, …
The actual next character supplies the training target.
caption: Illustrative possibilities, not predictions from a running model. The task is to assign probabilities, not to find one universally correct continuation.
build: Start with a character-count baseline: count what follows each character, then turn those counts into probabilities. This bigram model sees only the last character.
how: Conditional probability means ‘how likely is this next token, given the context?’ A baseline makes that question concrete before we introduce a neural network.
checkpoint: Why can two different continuations both be reasonable?
answer: A prefix rarely determines a unique continuation. The model represents uncertainty with a distribution over possible next tokens.
next: To compute with these possibilities, we need to represent text as numbers.

title: Represent
question: How can a model work with text?
what: A tokenizer splits text into tokens and assigns each one an ID. A learned embedding then maps an ID to a vector that the model can transform.
why: Text needs a consistent numerical representation before a model can calculate with it. Token IDs identify symbols; embeddings give the model adjustable representations.
example: Embedding lookup: one learned vector per ID
caption: A toy vocabulary: c = 0, a = 1, t = 2. These IDs do not mean that t is twice as meaningful as a. Decoding the IDs returns the original text.
build: Create a character vocabulary, encode/decode functions, and fixed-length text windows. Pair each input position with the next character as its target. Reserve validation text before fitting the model.
how: An embedding is a lookup table of trainable numbers. Matrix operations combine those representations. Position information will later tell attention where each token occurs.
checkpoint: Would renumbering the vocabulary change the meaning of the text?
answer: No, provided encoding, decoding, and the model’s lookup entries remain consistent. IDs are labels, not measures of meaning.
next: A representation alone does not make useful predictions. Its parameters need to learn from examples.

title: Learn
question: How do predictions get better?
what: The model predicts a distribution for each training example. A loss measures how poorly it predicted the observed next token. Training adjusts parameters to reduce that loss.
why: Writing rules for every possible sentence is impractical. An adjustable model can learn statistical patterns from many examples instead.
example: Predict probabilities for the next token
Measure loss against the observed token
caption: For next-token training, cross-entropy rewards assigning more probability to the observed token. One update need not improve every individual example.
build: Replace fixed counts with trainable next-token scores. Convert scores to probabilities with softmax, calculate cross-entropy, and optimize the parameters. Compare training loss with loss on reserved validation text.
how: Gradients describe how parameters affect loss. Backpropagation computes those gradients through chained operations; an optimizer uses them to update parameters. We can write the model and training loop while using automatic differentiation for the gradients.
checkpoint: Does lower training loss guarantee better predictions on new text?
answer: No. A model can fit training examples without generalizing. Reserved validation data helps reveal that gap.
next: The model can now learn, but a last-character baseline misses longer relationships. It needs more context.

title: Use context
question: Why does earlier text matter?
summary: Connect each token to what came before.
what: A useful next-token prediction depends on more than the last character. Causal attention lets a position combine information from positions up to and including itself, without looking at future targets.
why: Compare ‘the cat’ and ‘a hat’: both end in t, but the surrounding text differs. A last-character baseline gives them the same next-token distribution; a richer model can distinguish their contexts.
example: Future positions are masked during training
caption: Attention is learned weighting, not a guarantee that the model understands meaning. The causal mask prevents it from reading the answer ahead.
build: Add token and position embeddings, causal self-attention, and a feedforward network. Combine them with residual connections and normalization into a small decoder-only transformer block, then train it with the same next-token objective.
how: Queries and keys produce comparison scores; softmax turns them into weights; those weights combine values. Multiple heads provide several such computations. Feedforward layers transform the result; residual paths and normalization help make stacked blocks trainable.
checkpoint: Why hide future tokens if they already exist in the training text?
answer: At generation time, future tokens do not exist yet. Letting the model see them during training would teach it to use information it will not have when generating.
next: We have a model of the next token. Repeating that operation turns a prompt into a longer text.

title: Generate
question: How does prediction become text?
summary: Choose a token. Append it. Continue.
what: Give the model a prompt, sample a next token from its predicted distribution, append it, and run the model again with the updated context.
why: Repeated prediction turns a one-step model into a text generator. Sampling allows different continuations rather than always choosing the highest-probability token.
example: Sample one token → append to the prompt
Use the new context → predict again
caption: During ordinary generation the weights stay fixed. The text context changes. Temperature adjusts the sampling distribution, not what the model has learned.
build: Write a bounded generation loop with a token limit and context-window handling. Compare samples at different temperatures, and evaluate next-token loss on held-out text after model choices are settled.
how: Lower positive temperature concentrates probability on high-scoring tokens; higher temperature spreads it out. Samples reveal behavior, while held-out loss measures predictive performance. Neither alone establishes factual reliability.
checkpoint: Is the model learning new weights while it writes this paragraph?
answer: Not in this generation loop. Each chosen token changes the context used for the next prediction, while the trained parameters remain fixed.
next: The result: a tiny language model you can explain, train, and sample from. Better data, scale, and instruction tuning are later journeys.
